wine.name: Único
wine.grapes: Tinto Fino, the local Tempranillo, by far the larger part, with a small share of Cabernet Sauvignon.
wine.sites: Plots of the estate at Valbuena that lie between the slopes below the limestone plateau and the river's alluvial plain, at about 700 to 900 metres: fine colluvium with small fragments of limestone over sand and quartz gravel, with angular limestone stones on the surface.
wine.making: Fermented with native yeasts in wooden vats, where the malolactic follows. The wine then moves between barrels of 225 litres, French and American, new and used, and large wooden vats, five to six years in wood by the house's sheets and pages, then the rest of its time in bottle, so that it leaves the estate at least ten years after its harvest.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant and dried cherry over cedar, cigar box and a cool, minty lift, then tobacco, leather and polished wood; fine, silky tannin, fresh acidity and a long, fragrant finish.
wine.ageing: Already resolved when it is sold, a decade after the harvest, it keeps for decades more; the house speaks of forty to sixty years in a good cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant an older bottle gently off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The estate's first wine, sold about ten years after its harvest.
The Denominación de Origen of the upper Duero valley, created in 1982.
A different bottling: several vintages of Único blended and sold without a year.

records.table: From Valbuena de Duero, Vega Sicilia's Único is mostly Tinto Fino with a little Cabernet Sauvignon, held at least ten years between wood and bottle before it is sold. Cedar, tobacco and mint, already resolved, it asks only a gentle decant off its sediment.
records.story: The name Vega de Sicilia was first written for this stretch of the Duero in 1577, by the house's account. In 1848 the Lecanda family bought the estate from the Marquis of Valbuena, and in 1864 the buyer's son began to make wine here, planting cuttings from Bordeaux of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Malbec beside the local Tinto Fino. He was no trader, the house admits, and in 1888 the estate was sold to a man named Herrero; in 1897 another Herrero, no relation, bought it at auction. In 1907, as the house tells it, a Rioja merchant who leased the estate, seeking wine to make up for the phylloxera that had struck Rioja, hired a Basque winemaker to run its cellar, and the first Único is usually dated to the 1915 vintage. A seed company, Prodes, bought Vega Sicilia in 1950, and in 1965 it passed to a Venezuelan businessman of Czech origin who had tasted its wines in New York. In April 1982, the year Ribera del Duero became a Denominación de Origen, the Álvarez family bought the estate. Through every change of hands the wine kept its slow making, years in wood and years in bottle. For a sommelier Único is the lesson in patience: the red that made the valley's name long before the Denominación, sold only when it is ready.

questions.exp: The Álvarez family bought it in 1982; two unrelated Herreros held it from 1888, the second's family until the sale to Prodes in 1950, and the Lecandas founded it.

report: Searches for this record: eight of the group's 35, four restricted to the house's domain (temposvegasicilia.com) and one more on vegasicilia.com that gave nothing; no WebFetch tried.

The dates of 1577, 1848, 1864, 1888, 1897, 1907, 1950, 1965 and 1982 rest on the house's own history page and are hedged where they are its telling; 1982 also rests on El Español and Liv-ex, and the Bordeaux cuttings of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Malbec on Wikipedia and Best of Wines.

The founder (Eloy Lecanda y Chaves, the buyer's son) and his father, the Basque winemaker (Domingo Garramiola, called Txomin, dead in 1933 by one source), the Rioja merchant (Cosme Palacio) and the buyer of 1965 (Hans Neumann) are described, not named, since no source read gave their dates twice.

Garramiola's arrival is 1904 or 1905 in some accounts; the house's 1907 is kept and hedged. The first Único is 1915 in most accounts and 1915 or 1917 in Decántalo, so it is said to be usually dated to 1915; the recognition of the 1917 and 1918 at Barcelona in 1929 rests on one source and is left out.

Sites, the native yeasts, the barrels of 225 litres and the large vats, six years in wood and four in bottle, and forty to sixty years of life are the house's Único page and sheets; the grape share (92 to 96 per cent Tinto Fino in the sheets read) is said in words.

The library record calls the younger wine Valbuena 5o; the house prints the five with a small raised o, which the lint reads as a degree sign, so the record writes Valbuena 5. The library's note on Único uses the word benchmark, a judgement this tab refuses; nothing here depends on it.
No swap proposed. The living heads of the Álvarez family and the winemakers since 1982 are not named.

wine.name: Pingus
wine.grapes: Tinto Fino alone, the local name for Tempranillo.
wine.sites: Old bush vines at La Horra, farmed biodynamically, above all two neighbouring parcels, both planted in 1929: Barroso, on an old terrace of the Duero with gravel and sand over clay and limestone, and San Cristóbal, a clay slope facing south west.
wine.making: The old bush vines give low yields, and the wine is aged in new French oak barrels. From the late 2010s part of it has also rested in large oak vats beside the barrels.
wine.glass: Blackberry, black cherry and blueberry over violet, liquorice and graphite, with a flinty edge; opaque and dense yet polished, with fine, ripe tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Dense and closed in its first years, it opens slowly over a decade and keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead to let it open; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The estate's grand vin, from its old bush vines at La Horra.
The name of the estate: the domain of Pingus, after its founder's nickname.
The Denominación de Origen, where a red must be at least three quarters Tempranillo.

records.table: Old bush vines at La Horra, above all two parcels planted in 1929, give Dominio de Pingus its Pingus, Tinto Fino alone, raised in new French oak. Dense, dark and polished, with violet and graphite, it is the modern face of Ribera beside the long aged Único.
records.story: A young Danish winemaker came to Ribera del Duero in the early 1990s to build up the cellar of a new estate, Hacienda Monasterio. He turned to the old bush vines of La Horra, and in 1995 he made the first Pingus from two parcels there, Barroso and San Cristóbal, both planted in 1929. He named the wine after his own childhood nickname. An American critic praised the 1995, and the story goes that part of that small first vintage was lost when the ship carrying it to America sank off the Azores, though the accounts differ on the year. Flor de Pingus, from a wider set of vineyards around La Horra, became the second wine, and the vines came to be farmed biodynamically. Later the founder began PSI, a project with the valley's growers that buys their old vine fruit so that their vineyards are worked rather than pulled up. From the late 2010s part of Pingus has rested in large oak vats beside the new barrels. For a sommelier Pingus is the other pole of Ribera: where Único is made by years in the cellar, Pingus is made by old vines and low yields, and its 1995 showed that the valley had more than one house to know.

No WebFetch tried; every other fact stands on two secondary sources.

The founder, his wife and the estate's team are living and not named; the founder's name is already in people.json, and an address carrying it (the Académie du Vin, Decanter and Corney and Barrow profiles read through search) is not used as a source.

Barroso and San Cristóbal, neighbouring and both planted in 1929, rest on Corney and Barrow, the Rare Wine Co technical sheet and Vila Viniteca; their soils (Barroso an old Duero terrace of gravel and sand over clay and limestone, San Cristóbal a clay slope facing south west) on Vila Viniteca and a second merchant. Their sizes differ between sources and are not given. Decanter's Spanish Icons and the Rare Wine Co sheet were read through search and are not listed for want of room.
The ship story is told as a story: Wikipedia gives 75 of the first cases lost off the Azores in November 1997, another account the whole vintage in 1998, and a third calls it a myth.

Large oak vats rest on Berry Bros (first used for the 2018) and a review of the 2020 (starting that year), so the record says the late 2010s and gives no size; new French oak rests on Millesima and Westgarth. Wooden fermenters (the Rare Wine Co sheet alone), wild yeasts, the months in barrel and the start of biodynamic farming (2000 in one merchant's page) were not found twice and are left out.
Flor de Pingus's first vintage (1996 in Decanter) and PSI's dates (begun in 2006, first vintage 2007, Decanter alone) are left out.
The library's Spain's modern cult wine is a judgement this tab refuses; the American critics' praise of the 1995 is told without a score or a name, on Wikipedia and Decanter.

wine.name: Tinto Pesquera Reserva
wine.classification: Reserva: at least three years of ageing, one of them in oak barrels
wine.grapes: Tinto Fino alone, the local Tempranillo, with no Bordeaux grape in the blend.
wine.sites: The family's own vineyards around Pesquera de Duero, in the Valladolid stretch of the valley, planted to Tinto Fino alone.
wine.making: The wine is aged at least fourteen months in American oak barrels of 225 litres, by the house's own sheets, then rested in bottle before it is sold. The Denominación asks a Reserva for three years of ageing with at least twelve months in oak.
wine.glass: Blackberry, plum and black cherry over vanilla, cocoa and tobacco, with the dill and coconut American oak can give; firm, dusty tannin and a warm, toasty finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and oak marked on release, it softens over five to ten years and holds well beyond.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Aged at least three years, a year or more of it in oak barrels.
The name of the wine and the house, after the village of Pesquera de Duero.

records.table: Founded in 1972 in the village whose name it carries, Tinto Pesquera makes its Reserva from Tinto Fino alone and ages it in American oak: blackberry, vanilla and tobacco over firm, dusty tannin, the Ribera that went abroad beside Vega Sicilia in the 1980s.
records.story: Alejandro Fernández (1932 to 2021) and his wife were both born in Pesquera de Duero, a village on the river in the Valladolid stretch of the valley. With money from the sale of a patent, by the family's account, they bought a small sixteenth century stone press house in the village, and there in 1972 they began to make wine of Tinto Fino alone from the family's vines; the first Tinto Pesquera, named for their village, came from the 1975 vintage. Fernández was among the growers who pressed for a Denominación de Origen, and when the ministry's order of 21 July 1982 created Ribera del Duero it counted about ten wineries. In the middle of the 1980s an American critic praised the house's 1982 wines, likening them to Pétrus, and Pesquera found its way onto wine lists abroad beside Vega Sicilia. The house kept to its first idea, Tinto Fino alone and American oak, while French oak became the modern habit of the valley. The family went on to build other wineries, Condado de Haza at Roa among them, and Fernández died in Santander in May 2021, aged 88. For a sommelier the Reserva is Ribera as its first modern generation made it: one grape, American oak and the name of a village on the label.

report: Searches for this record: seven of the group's 35, one of them restricted to the family's domain (familiafernandezrivera.com), beside the one on the Denominación's rules (riberadelduero.es) that serves the whole group; no WebFetch tried.

Alejandro Fernández's dates rest on Spanish Wine Lover (1932 to 2021), Wine Industry Advisor and Wein.plus (died in Santander on 22 May 2021, aged 88); Wein.plus was read through search and is not listed for want of room. His wife, who co-founded the house, and his daughters, who have led the family's group since 2019, are not named; the wife's status was not settled, so she is described.

The stone press house of 1972, bought with the sale of a patent, both founders born in the village and the first wines of 1975 rest on the family's own history and Tinto Pesquera pages, with Spanish Wine Lover and Wein.plus beside them (one hotel news item of the group says 1974); the American critic's praise of the 1982 wines likened to Pétrus on two accounts that differ on whether it was the 1982 Janus or the 1982 vintage, so the story says the house's 1982 wines. The critic is not named.

The Reserva's oak is given as fourteen months to two years because the sheets read differ (14 in Bodeboca and one review, 24 in Monsieur Touton, En Copa de Balón and Gourmet Hunters, some with French oak in the 2019); about a year in bottle is the importers' figure.

The order of 21 July 1982 and about ten wineries rest on the Consejo Regulador's own pages (its history of the region at riberadelduero.es/en/node/2465 and the 40th anniversary notes); the Reserva and Gran Reserva rules on its Pliego de condiciones.

Left out for want of a second independent source: what the patent was for, farm machinery for sugar beet growers (Spanish Wine Lover's two pages only), his Gold Medal of Merit in Labour of 2014, and the first Janus of 1982.

Condado de Haza at Roa and Janus as the house's Gran Reserva rest on the library record alone, which also names the house Bodegas Alejandro Fernández Tinto Pesquera; recent bottles are sold under the family's group, Familia Fernández Rivera.

wine.name: Protos Gran Reserva
wine.classification: Gran Reserva: at least five years of ageing, two of them in oak barrels
wine.grapes: Tinto Fino alone, the local Tempranillo.
wine.sites: Small parcels of very old Tinto Fino in the valley, the vines more than sixty years old by the house's sheet.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel at 26 to 28 degrees Celsius, with three to four weeks on the skins. It then spends at least twenty four months in oak barrels, about four fifths French and the rest American, most of them new, and at least thirty six months in bottle before it is sold.
wine.glass: Deep cherry red with a garnet rim; fruit compote, cocoa, dark chocolate and roasted coffee over tobacco, toast and a light smoke, with round tannin and a long, silky finish.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink when it is released, after five years and more in the cellars, it has by the house's own note a long life ahead in bottle.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, as the house advises; decant gently off any sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: The Peñafiel house that gave Ribera del Duero its name in 1982, Protos ages its Gran Reserva two years in mostly French oak and three in bottle, so the Tinto Fino arrives mellow, with cocoa, tobacco and toast. Pour it beside roast lamb.
records.story: In March 1927, by the house's account, eleven growers of Peñafiel, friends since childhood, joined to found a winery in the town, and its first wines, of 1927 and 1928, won gold medals at the Barcelona exposition of 1929. It traded under the name Ribera Duero. About 1970 the house dug an ageing cellar into the hill beneath Peñafiel's castle, with more than two kilometres of galleries. When the Denominación de Origen was created in 1982, the winery, then a co-operative by the regulating council's own account, let the new council use its registered name, Ribera Duero, for the whole region, and took for itself the name Protos, the Greek word for first, in keeping with its motto, Ser Primero, to be first. In 2008 the house opened a new winery near the old, designed by the British architects Rogers Stirk Harbour and Partners with Alonso Balaguer and Arquitectos Asociados. The Gran Reserva keeps the long view of the founders' cellar: two years and more in barrel and three in bottle before it is sold. For a sommelier Protos is the house that gave the region its name, and its Gran Reserva is Ribera in its classical form, released only when long rested.

report: Searches for this record: six of the group's 35, three restricted to the house's domain (bodegasprotos.com); no WebFetch tried.

The founding of March 1927 by eleven growers, the gold medals of 1929 for the 1927 and 1928, the cellar dug about 1970 with more than two kilometres of galleries, the name Ribera Duero given to the Consejo Regulador in 1982 and the winery of 2008 rest on the house's own history, press notes and shop; the winery of 2008 also on Metalocus and Archello (built by September 2008, first harvest in October, left out of the story as a detail of one architecture account).

The name as the Greek for first rests on Decanter China (a promotional feature) and Vinissimus, with the house's motto Ser Primero beside them; one merchant gives the old name in full as Bodega Ribera Duero de Peñafiel, which the record does not print.

The Gran Reserva's making (steel at 26 to 28 degrees, three to four weeks on the skins, at least 24 months in barrels about 80 per cent French and 20 American, mostly new, at least 36 in bottle), its vines of more than sixty years and its serving at 16 to 18 degrees are the house's own sheet and shop.

The plan calls Protos a co-operative and the first winery named in Ribera; the house's pages read call the founders eleven growers and friends, and none gave the legal form, so the record does not say co-operative. The house's slogan, the first in the Ribera, is a claim about the name and not a first winery, since Vega Sicilia made wine from 1864; the record makes no claim of a first.
The architect Richard Rogers is dead (1933 to 2021) but only his firm is named, as the house names it.
No swap proposed; nobody living is named.

wine.name: Aalto PS
wine.grapes: Tinto Fino alone, the local Tempranillo.
wine.sites: Very old vines, sixty to a hundred years old by the house's sheets, from selected sites in La Horra and La Aguilera, with Fresnillo de las Dueñas in some years.
wine.making: The malolactic fermentation takes place in new barrels, and the wine is then aged in new French oak barrels for about twenty months, nineteen to twenty four by the house's sheets, before it is bottled.
wine.glass: Liquorice, Indian ink and flint over very ripe blackberry, with toast, coffee and tobacco from the new oak; dense and powerful, its tannin round despite the intensity.
wine.ageing: Dense and marked by its oak when young, it needs several years in bottle and keeps for two decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Pagos Seleccionados: the selected sites, the house's wine of very old vines.
The Denominación de Origen of the upper Duero valley, for reds mostly of Tempranillo.

records.table: Aalto PS, for Pagos Seleccionados, gathers Tinto Fino from very old vines at La Horra and La Aguilera, with its malolactic in new barrels and its ageing in new French oak: liquorice, Indian ink and ripe blackberry. Decant it an hour ahead.
records.story: Aalto began in February 1999, the work of two men who knew Ribera del Duero from the inside: a winemaker who had run the cellar of Vega Sicilia for some thirty years, until 1998, and a former head of the Denominación's regulating council. They set out to gather old vines from many villages of the valley rather than to farm a single estate, and until the 2004 harvest the house made its wines in rented premises at Roa. Its own winery at Quintanilla de Arriba, in Valladolid, built in stages, was ready in part for the 2005 harvest, and in 2006 the Masaveu and Nozaleda families joined the venture. A second stage, built for visitors, followed in 2016. Beside Aalto, the house's broader red, stands the selection called PS, for Pagos Seleccionados, the chosen sites: Tinto Fino from very old vines in villages such as La Horra and La Aguilera, with its malolactic in new barrels and its ageing in new French oak. For a sommelier Aalto PS is the classical training of Vega Sicilia's cellar turned to the old vines of many villages: a modern Ribera with long experience behind it.

others.note: The house's broader red, Tinto Fino from many villages of the valley, a wider blend of sites than PS.

questions.exp: The house's sheets give the malolactic in new barrels and about twenty months in new French oak; years in large vats and a decade before release are Vega Sicilia's way with Único.

questions.exp: From 1999 until the 2004 harvest the house worked in rented premises at Roa; its own winery at Quintanilla de Arriba took its first harvest in 2005.

report: Searches for this record: five of the group's 35, three restricted to the house's domain (aalto.es); no WebFetch tried.

The founding of February 1999, the rented premises at Roa until the 2004 harvest, the first stage of the winery finished for the 2005 harvest, the families who joined in 2006 and the second stage of 2016 rest on the house's own pages and dossier; 1999 and the Roa years also on European Cellars and Wine with Seth.

The founders are described, not named: the winemaker who ran Vega Sicilia's cellar for thirty years until 1998 is living and in people.json; the second, a former director or president of the Consejo Regulador (the sources differ on the title, so the story says head), is given as 1954 to 2023 by one source only, so he is described and no dates are given.

PS as Pagos Seleccionados rests on the importers Trialto and European Cellars; the sites (vines of 60 to 90 years at La Horra and La Aguilera, with Fresnillo or Piñel de Abajo in some years), the malolactic in new barrels and 18 to 22 months in new French oak are the house's sheets of 2009 to 2023.
The glass draws on the sheets' liquorice, Indian ink, flint, toast, coffee and tobacco; the sheets say black fruit, given here as blackberry.
Left out: the year of the first PS (a 2001 is the earliest the results named), one founder's departure in 2018 (one source), and the house's later winemakers, who are living.
No swap proposed.
